Set a random seed before each simulation question and report it. You may use standard packages unless a question asks you to write the calculation yourself. Use equal neighbor weights throughout. Here pp counts the covariates used to measure distance; do not add an intercept column to a KNN predictor matrix. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact simulation results need not agree.

Question 1: Estimate the bias and variance of KNN

In our previous homework, we used repeated simulations to study the behavior of linear regression estimators. We will now use the same idea for KNN. Consider the regression model

Yi=f(𝐗i)+ϵi,f(𝐱)=0.5x1+sin⁡(x2)−0.3x32, Y_i=f(\mathbf X_i)+\epsilon_i, \qquad f(\mathbf x)=0.5x_1+\sin(x_2)-0.3x_3^2,

where the three covariates are independent standard normal variables and ϵi∼𝒩(0,0.12)\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2) independently of the covariates and other observations. Generate n=400n=400 training observations. Our goal is to estimate the mean response at

𝐱0=(0.5,0.7,1)𝖳. \mathbf x_0=(0.5,0.7,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Use Euclidean distance and consider k=1,3,5,…,29k=1,3,5,\ldots,29.

  1. Calculate f(𝐱0)f(\mathbf x_0). Generate one training dataset and obtain the KNN prediction at 𝐱0\mathbf x_0 for each value of kk.

  2. Independently repeat the generation of the training covariates and responses 200 times. Within each repetition, use the same training data for every value of kk. Store the predictions in a matrix with 200 rows and one column for each value of kk. Use this matrix to estimate the bias, variance, and mean squared error of the estimated mean response. Use divisor 200 when calculating the empirical variance, and verify numerically that

mean squared error=squared bias+variance. \text{mean squared error} =\text{squared bias}+\text{variance}.

Plot squared bias, variance, and mean squared error against kk in one figure. Explain the pattern and compare it with the bias-variance trade-off for ridge regression or lasso.

Show the workflow 
library(kknn)
set.seed(54782)
n <- 400
p <- 3
k_val <- seq(1, 29, 2)
x0 <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.7, 1))
x0 <- t(x0)
f0 <-  0.5 * x0[1, 1] + sin(x0[1, 2]) - 0.3 * (x0[1, 3])^2

X <- matrix(rnorm(n*p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
y <- 0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * (X[, 3])^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)

prediction <- numeric(length(k_val))

for (i in seq_along(k_val)) {
  k <- k_val[i]
  knn.fit <- kknn(y ~ ., train = data.frame("x" = X, "y" = y), 
                  test = data.frame("x" = x0), k = k, kernel = "rectangular", scale = FALSE)
  prediction[i] <- knn.fit$fitted.values
}

par(old_par)

Variance generally decreases as kk increases because with larger k, it averages more responses; but it also includes observations farther from the target in predictor space, increasing squared bias. MSE initially decreases until it hits its lowest MSE at k=7k = 7 among the tested values. For larger kk, MSE generally increases. The identity check differences are really small, effectively zero, so it supports the idea of MSE = squared bias + variance.

Increasing kk has a similar effect to increasing the penalty in ridge and lasso regressions. The predictions become less flexible and trade-offs between bias and variance do exist. For ridge and lasso, when penalty increases, variance generally decreases and squared bias generally increases. That is similar to the KNN as when kk increases, variance also generally decreases and squared bias also generally increases.

Question 2: Compare KNN with lasso

Use the response model from Question 1, including the noise standard deviation 0.10.1, but generate p=30p=30 covariates. The response still depends only on the first three. Consider these two settings:

  • Setting 1: all 30 covariates are independent standard normal variables.

  • Setting 2: the covariates have a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, where

    Σjj=1,Σjl=0.8for j≠l. \Sigma_{jj}=1, \qquad \Sigma_{jl}=0.8\quad\text{for }j\ne l.

In each setting, generate 400 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations. Fit 5NN using Euclidean distance on the supplied covariate scale. All covariates already have population variance one.

For lasso, use a linear model containing the 30 covariates and a separately fitted, unpenalized intercept. Follow the Week 4 objective,

Lλ(𝛃)=12n∥𝐲̃−𝐗𝛃∥22+λ‖𝛃‖1, L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) =\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 +\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1,

where 𝐗∈ℝn×30\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times30} contains the centered and standardized covariates and 𝐲̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the centered training response. Select the penalty by ten-fold cross-validation over 41 logarithmically spaced values from 10−410^{-4} to 11. Estimate all means and scales using only the training portion of each fold, with divisor equal to that portion’s sample size. After selecting the penalty, refit on all training observations and apply the fitted transformations unchanged to the test observations. Do not add nonlinear terms to the lasso model.

  1. Fit both methods in each setting. Use the same training and test data for the two methods within a setting. Report their test MSE values in one table, together with the selected lasso penalty and the number of nonzero lasso slopes. You only need to generate one dataset for each setting; repeated simulations are not required.

  2. Compare the results between the two settings. Explain how correlation can change the usefulness of Euclidean neighborhoods, and why lasso does not use all covariates in the same way as KNN.

  3. The response model contains sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, but the lasso fit uses only linear terms. Explain how this difference affects the comparison. Would the results justify a general claim that correlation always helps KNN, or that one method is always better? Explain why.

Show the workflow 
library(kknn)
library(glmnet)
Loading required package: Matrix
Loaded glmnet 5.0
Show the workflow 
set.seed(54782)
n <- 400
n_test <- 1000
p <- 30
k <- 5

# setting 1
x_test <- matrix(rnorm(n_test * p), nrow = n_test, ncol = p)
x <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
y_train <- 0.5 * x[, 1] + sin(x[, 2]) - 0.3 * (x[, 3])^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)
y_test <- 0.5 * x_test[, 1] + sin(x_test[, 2]) - 0.3 * (x_test[, 3])^2 + rnorm(n_test, sd = 0.1)

knn.fit <- kknn(y ~ ., train = data.frame("x" = x, "y" = y_train), 
                  test = data.frame("x" = x_test), k = 5, kernel = "rectangular", scale = FALSE)

pred <- knn.fit$fitted.values

test_mse_knn <- mean((y_test - pred)^2)

lambda <- 10^seq(0, -4, length.out = 41)

fold <- rep(NA_integer_, n)
fold[seq_len(n)] <- sample(rep(1:10, each = n / 10))

fit <- cv.glmnet(
  x = x,
  y = y_train,
  family = "gaussian",
  alpha = 1,
  lambda = lambda,
  foldid = fold,
  type.measure = "mse",
  standardize = TRUE
)

min_lambda <- fit$lambda.min

y_hat <- predict(fit, newx = x_test, s = min_lambda)

test_mse_lasso <- mean((y_test - y_hat)^2)

c <- coef(fit, s = min_lambda)
slopes <- c[-1, 1]
nonzero_count <- sum(slopes != 0)
nonzero_count
[1] 6
Show the workflow 
# setting 2
covariance <- matrix(0.8, nrow = 30, ncol = 30)
diag(covariance) <- 1

x_cor <- x %*% chol(covariance)
x_test_cor <- x_test %*% chol(covariance)

y_train_cor <- 0.5 * x_cor[, 1] + sin(x_cor[, 2]) -
  0.3 * x_cor[, 3]^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)

y_test_cor <- 0.5 * x_test_cor[, 1] + sin(x_test_cor[, 2]) -
  0.3 * x_test_cor[, 3]^2 + rnorm(n_test, sd = 0.1)

pred_2 <- knn.fit_2$fitted.values

test_mse_knn_2 <- mean((y_test_cor - pred_2)^2)

Show the workflow 
results <- data.frame(
  Setting = c("Independent", "Correlated"),
  KNN_MSE = c(test_mse_knn, test_mse_knn_2), Lasso_MSE = c(test_mse_lasso, test_mse_lasso_2),
  Lambda = c(min_lambda, min_lambda_2), Nonzero = c(nonzero_count, nonzero_count_2)
)

knitr::kable(results, digits = 3)
Setting KNN_MSE Lasso_MSE Lambda Nonzero
Independent 0.600 0.300 0.040 6
Correlated 0.188 0.276 0.025 4
  1. With independent covariates, KNN’s test mse is larger than lasso’s. On the other hand, with correlated covariates, lasso’s test mse is larger than KNN’s. When the predictors were correlated, KNN’s test MSE changed from 0.600 to 0.188, while lasso’s changed from 0.300 to 0.276. KNN measures distance using all 30 predictors, including the 27 outside the response formula. So with independent covariates, many coordinates that do not affect the response contribute to Euclidean distance. Those extra predictors can make observations look far apart even when their first three predictors are similar. Strong correlation makes the predictors more redundant, which can make neighborhoods more useful here.

Unlike KNN’s use of every coordinate, lasso shrinks the slopes and can set them to zero. Lasso can reduce or eliminate a predictor’s contribution by shrinking its coefficient toward or to zero, although it does not necessarily remove every predictor outside the true response formula.

  1. Because the lasso model uses only linear terms, it can’t fully represent the non-linear terms in the response formula, which can introduce bias in its predictions. Therefore, this comparison reflects both the methods and the restrictions of the lasso model. These results do not establish that either method is always better than the other because the better-performing method changed between settings, and only one dataset was simulated per setting. KNN’s accuracy depends on whether it finds useful neighbors, and correlation does not guarantee that nearby observations will have similar mean responses. Although correlation helped KNN in this simulation, it may not help with other response functions or correlation structures. Therefore, these results do not show that correlation always helps KNN.

Question 3: Observed dimension and latent dimension

The lecture’s handwritten digit example shows that KNN can work with many measured covariates. We will use a simulation to investigate why the structure of those covariates matters.

Let p=100p=100 be the number of observed covariates and let mm be the number of latent variables. For each observation, generate

𝐗i=𝐀𝐙i+𝛈i,Yi=Zi1+Zi2+ϵi, \mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i+\boldsymbol\eta_i, \qquad Y_i=Z_{i1}+Z_{i2}+\epsilon_i,

where 𝐀∈ℝ100×m\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{100\times m} has independent entries from Uniform[−2,2][-2,2]. The entries of 𝐙i∈ℝm\mathbf Z_i\in\mathbb R^m and 𝛈i∈ℝ100\boldsymbol\eta_i\in\mathbb R^{100}, and the scalar ϵi\epsilon_i, are independent standard normal variables, also independent of 𝐀\mathbf A. Generate 𝐀\mathbf A once and use it for all training and test observations in that dataset.

Compare m=3m=3 and m=30m=30. In each setting, generate 200 training observations and 200 independent test observations. Fit KNN using only the 100 observed covariates in 𝐗\mathbf X, with Euclidean distance on their generated scale. The latent variables in 𝐙\mathbf Z are used to generate the data but are not available to the fitted model. Consider k=2,10,18,…,82k=2,10,18,\ldots,82.

  1. Generate one dataset for each value of mm. Fit KNN for every value of kk and calculate test MSE. Within a setting, use the same training and test observations for all values of kk.

  2. Repeat the complete experiment 50 times, generating a new 𝐀\mathbf A and new observations in each repetition. Plot average test MSE against kk, with one curve for each value of mm. These curves compare the specified choices of kk in a controlled simulation; they are not a cross-validation procedure for selecting a final model.

  3. Both settings have 100 observed covariates, and the response depends on only two latent variables. Explain why their KNN performance can still differ. What role does the noise 𝛈i\boldsymbol\eta_i play, and why are the observed data not confined exactly to an mm-dimensional linear space?

Show the workflow 
library(kknn)
set.seed(54782)

# part a
n <- 200
p <- 100
m_val <- c(3, 30)
k_val <- seq(2, 82, 8)
test_mse <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(k_val), ncol = 2)

for (m in m_val) {
  A <- matrix(runif(p*m, -2, 2), nrow = p, ncol = m)
  Z <- matrix(rnorm(n*2*m), nrow = n*2, ncol = m)
  X <- Z %*% t(A) + matrix(rnorm(n*2*p), nrow = n*2, ncol = p)
  y <- Z[, 1] + Z[, 2] + rnorm(n*2)

  for (k in k_val) {
    knn.fit <- kknn(y ~ ., train = data.frame("x" = X[1:200, ], "y" = y[1:200]), 
                  test = data.frame("x" = X[201:400, ]), k = k, kernel = "rectangular", scale = FALSE)

    test_mse[match(k, k_val), match(m, m_val)] <- 
      mean((y[201:400] - knn.fit$fitted.values)^2)
  }
}

result <- data.frame(k = k_val, m3 = test_mse[, 1], m30 = test_mse[, 2])

Although both settings have 100 observed predictors, the setting with m=3m = 3 has lower average test mse. When m=3m = 3, the latent variables are Z1,Z2,Z3Z_1, Z_2, Z_3. The response formula depends on Z1Z_1 and Z2Z_2, so there’s only one latent variable outside the response formula. With m=30m = 30, there are 28 other latent variables that influence the observed predictors. Those extra latent variables affect distances between observations even though they don’t affect the mean response. This can make observations with similar mean responses appear far apart, making useful neighbors harder to find.

The predictor noise adds variation in all 100 coordinates and can make distances less informative. Without this noise, 𝐀𝐙𝐢\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z_i} lies in the space spanned by the mm columns of 𝐀\mathbf{A}. Adding noise pushes observations outside that space, so the observed data are not confined exactly to an (m)-dimensional linear space.

Question 4: Classify handwritten digits

Use zip.train and zip.test from the R package ElemStatLearn, as in the lecture. The package has been retired from the active CRAN repository. If needed, install the archived package into your usual R library, then load the two datasets. Python users can use the course copies of the same training data and test data. These compressed CSV files have no headers and are included in the homework ZIP under data/knn. Run the Python code from the folder containing data.

Each image has 16×16=25616\times16=256 pixel values. The first column is the digit label and the remaining columns are the pixel values. Use the first 1,000 rows of zip.train and the first 500 rows of zip.test. Use the original pixel values without standardization, and do not include the digit label in a distance calculation.

For a test image 𝐱0\mathbf x_0 and a training image 𝐱i\mathbf x_i, the two distances are

dE(𝐱0,𝐱i)=∑j=1256(x0j−xij)2,dM(𝐱0,𝐱i)=∑j=1256|x0j−xij|. d_E(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{256}(x_{0j}-x_{ij})^2}, \qquad d_M(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sum_{j=1}^{256}|x_{0j}-x_{ij}|.

  1. Write a 5NN classification function that allows either Euclidean or Manhattan distance. For each test image, calculate its distances to the training images directly, find the five nearest, and return the most frequent digit label. Break distance ties by the smaller training row number and voting ties by the smallest digit. Do not use a built-in distance or KNN function for this part.

  2. Apply the classifier to all 500 test images using each distance. For each fit, report the test classification error and a 10×1010\times10 confusion matrix, with rows representing predicted digits and columns representing true digits. Keep all digit labels from 0 through 9 in the matrix, including any with a zero count. Which digits are most often confused with one another?

  3. For Euclidean distance, display three incorrectly classified test images, together with their true and predicted labels. Comment on whether the mistakes are visually understandable. Compare the overall results of the two distance measures. Can they have similar total error while making mistakes on different images? Use your predictions to support your answer.

Show the workflow 
library(ElemStatLearn)
data(zip.train)
data(zip.test)

x_train <- zip.train[1:1000, -1]
y_train <- zip.train[1:1000, 1]
x_test <- zip.test[1:500, -1]
y_test <- zip.test[1:500, 1]

euclidean_distance <- function(x0, x) {
  sqrt(rowSums(sweep(x, 2, x0, "-")^2))
}

manhattan_distance <- function(x0, x) {
  rowSums(abs(sweep(x, 2, x0, "-")))
}

knn_classify <- function(x_train, y_train, x_test, distance) {
  predictions <- integer(nrow(x_test))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(x_test))) {
    d <- distance(x_test[i, ], x_train)
    neighbor <- order(d, seq_len(nrow(x_train)))[1:5]
    neighbor_labels <- y_train[neighbor]
    votes <- table(factor(neighbor_labels, levels = 0:9))
    predictions[i] <- which.max(votes) - 1
  }
  return(predictions)
}

pred_euclidean <- knn_classify(x_train, y_train, x_test, euclidean_distance)

The most frequent confusion is a true 2 predicted as a 0. There are seven images under the euclidean distance, and there are six images under the manhattan distance.

The mistakes are somewhat understandable because the digits are written in unusual ways. The 6 has a round loop that looks like a 0, and the 2 also has a curved shape. The 4 being predicted as a 7 is harder to understand, but its slanted lines might explain the confusion.

Euclidean distance had a slightly lower error rate of 12.2%, compared to 13.8% for Manhattan distance. Both methods got 58 images wrong, while 3 were wrong only with Euclidean distance and 11 only with Manhattan distance. So even though their error rates are similar, they do not always make mistakes on the same images.

# STAT 432 Plot Formatting

Improve the requested plot's readability while preserving its data, calculations, and statistical meaning. Use the existing plotting library.

- Margins: leave enough space for titles, tick labels, axis labels, and legends without clipping or excessive blank space.
- Titles: use a short, descriptive title that identifies the comparison without claiming a result unsupported by the plot.
- Axes and labels: name the quantities clearly, include units when applicable, use readable tick spacing, and keep comparable panels on consistent scales when appropriate.
- Colors: use distinct, colorblind-friendly colors on a light background; distinguish curves with line styles or point shapes as well as color.
- Sizes: choose a figure size that is readable in the homework report; use legible text, moderately thick lines, and points that do not hide the curves. Start around 7 by 5 inches and 11-12 point text, adjusting to the plot.
- Legends: label every series clearly and place the legend where it does not cover data.
